<reason>CON (Side A) built and sustained the sharper route to victory: the conjunctive "only when, all three" gate either imposes real obligations that block low-risk venues (the jazz bar) or collapses into ornamental paperwork. PRO's answers to pressure did real damage to its own case — "merely listing a subway prevents nothing by itself," the protective mechanism named (staff directing patrons) is a conduct condition, extensions are "denied" when the agency stays silent, and PRO's closing offered employer-funded taxis as a plan, which CON plausibly noted occurs without any gate. PRO's best line — plans test readiness, inspections test delivery, and the community bears risk "before enforcement catches up" — was coherent and honestly argued, but PRO never specified what advance verification of a rota actually secures beyond a promise, leaving CON's "risk window identical" claim largely standing. CON answered PRO's pressure questions directly (including the honest "Yes" on approving despite a transit gap) and used its rebuttals to narrow and resolve the clash rather than repeat. CON's opening was clipped, a minor execution cost. Clear but competitive win for CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 exploiting B's pressure answers: PRO conceded the transit paragraph "prevents nothing by itself" and named staff directing patrons as the real protection; CON reframed that as a behavioural licence condition, added a dispersal radius to answer the "moves next door" worry, and concluded every protective element PRO named lives outside the plan wrapper — leaving the gate doing only two things, blocking venues for the city's failures and demanding documents where nothing is needed.</best_rebuttal>
